lines.text:
Fire from Below — Understanding Volcanoes

Deep beneath the Earth's surface, rock is so hot that it melts into a thick liquid called magma. When magma rises through cracks in the Earth's crust and reaches the surface, it erupts — and we call it a volcano.

The structure of a volcano is surprisingly simple. The cone is the mountain itself, built up over time by layers of cooled lava and ash. At the top, the crater — a bowl-shaped opening — is where the eruption happens. Below the crater, a vent connects the surface to the magma chamber deep underground. Some volcanoes have a caldera — a much larger depression formed when the top of the volcano collapses after a massive eruption. A lava tube — a natural tunnel formed when flowing lava cools on the surface but continues flowing underneath — can stretch for kilometres.

An eruption is one of nature's most powerful events. Magma becomes lava the moment it reaches the surface. A lava flow moves slowly downhill, destroying everything in its path. An ash cloud — a towering column of dust, gas, and rock fragments — can rise kilometres into the sky and block sunlight for days. A pyroclastic flow — a fast-moving cloud of superheated gas and rock — is the most dangerous part of an eruption, travelling at hundreds of kilometres per hour. A mudflow, created when volcanic ash mixes with rainwater, buries entire villages. Tremors and earthquakes shake the ground before, during, and after eruptions. A steam vent releases hot gas. Gas emissions — mostly carbon dioxide and sulphur — can be toxic.

Volcanoes create as well as destroy. The lava field around an old volcano eventually becomes some of the most fertile farmland on Earth. A volcanic island — like Hawaii or Iceland — is built entirely from eruptions on the ocean floor. A hot spring and a geyser — which shoots boiling water into the air — are heated by magma close to the surface. A fumarole releases steam and volcanic gas from cracks in the ground.

Volcanic rock tells the geological story. Basalt — dark, dense rock — forms when lava cools quickly on the surface. Obsidian — volcanic glass — is smooth and black. Pumice is so light that it floats on water because it is full of air bubbles. Granite forms deep underground when magma cools slowly. Tuff is made of compressed volcanic ash. Limestone, though not volcanic, is often found near ancient volcanic sites. Mineral crystals grow in volcanic cavities. Fossils in nearby rock show what lived before the eruption.

Scientists called volcanologists monitor active volcanoes using specialised equipment. A seismograph detects tremors and earthquakes. A tiltmeter measures changes in the volcano's shape. A gas analyser samples the air near vents. A thermal camera detects heat changes. A GPS station tracks ground movement. A weather station monitors wind direction — critical for predicting where ash clouds will travel. A drone flies over the crater when it is too dangerous for people. Satellite images provide a wide view. A sample kit collects rock, ash, and gas for laboratory analysis. A radiation detector checks for unusual emissions.

A mountain peak, a valley, a cliff, a cave, a lake, a steam cloud, a black sand beach — the landscape around a volcano is shaped entirely by fire from below.

lines.text: 'Many' + countable plural: 'many buildings', 'many people.' 'Much' + uncountable: 'much damage', 'much destruction.' In positive sentences, 'a lot of' works for both: 'a lot of buildings', 'a lot of damage.' 'Much' is mainly used in negative sentences and questions.

lines.text: 'Yesterday' = specific past time → use past simple: 'I saw it yesterday.' Present perfect ('I have seen') is used without a specific finished time: 'I have seen many documentaries about volcanoes.' Time markers like 'yesterday', 'last week', 'in 2023' always take past simple.

lines.text: '-ing' = describes the thing causing fear: 'The eruption was frightening.' '-ed' = describes how the person feels: 'Everyone was frightened.' The eruption causes fear (frightening); the people feel fear (frightened). This -ed/-ing pattern works with all emotion adjectives.
